about: West End and Holborn: a meeting off Regent Street, lunch on Oxford Street, an errand in Hatton Garden, dinner in Stoke Newington.

cards.line: Did you know, the Rolling Stones played their first ever gig on Oxford Street?
cards.fact: On 12 July 1962 the Rolling Stones played their first live show at the Marquee Club, then in a basement under a cinema on Oxford Street. The club moved to Wardour Street in 1964.

cards.line: Did you know, the Hatton Garden burglars got into the vault down a lift shaft?
cards.fact: Over the Easter weekend of 2015, a gang climbed down a lift shaft into a Hatton Garden safe deposit vault and drilled through its wall with an industrial drill. They took up to £14 million.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Hatton Garden safe deposit burglary

cards.line: Did you know, Edgar Allan Poe went to school in Stoke Newington?
cards.fact: The American writer Edgar Allan Poe was a pupil at the Manor House School on Church Street, Stoke Newington, around 1818, while his foster parents were living in Britain.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Edgar Allan Poe; Stoke Newington

cards.line: Did you know, the Ziggy Stardust album cover was shot in a little street off Regent Street?
cards.fact: In January 1972 David Bowie posed outside number 23 Heddon Street for the cover of Ziggy Stardust. Fans still photograph themselves on the doorstep, and a plaque now marks the spot.
cards.source: Wikipedia: The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars

cards.line: Did you know, Jimi Hendrix lived next door to Handel's house on Brook Street?
cards.fact: Jimi Hendrix lived at 23 Brook Street in 1968 and 1969. Next door, at number 25, the composer Handel had lived from 1723 until 1759. Today the two houses are one museum.

about: Knightsbridge shopping, Earl's Court, then Notting Hill and Portobello Road.

cards.line: Did you know, Monty Python started in a flat on Basil Street?
cards.fact: In the 1960s, the first meetings that led to Monty Python's Flying Circus were held in a flat on Basil Street, Knightsbridge.

cards.line: Did you know, one of the biggest robberies in history happened in a Knightsbridge side street?
cards.fact: In July 1987 two men entered a safe deposit centre in Cheval Place asking to rent a box. They left with about £60 million, one of the largest robberies in history.

cards.line: Did you know, Bob Marley gave police a false address on Collingham Gardens?
cards.fact: When Bob Marley was arrested for cannabis in 1977, he gave police an address on Collingham Gardens. It wasn't his home: he gave it to keep police away from where he lived, on Oakley Street.

cards.line: Did you know, the Kray twins once owned a Knightsbridge nightclub?
cards.fact: From 1960 to 1963 the Kray twins owned Esmeralda's Barn, a nightclub on Wilton Place in Knightsbridge. The gangsters used it to move their business into the West End.

cards.line: Did you know, the blue door from the film Notting Hill belonged to the man who wrote it?
cards.fact: Hugh Grant's house in the 1999 film Notting Hill is 280 Westbourne Park Road, owned by the film's writer, Richard Curtis. The blue door was auctioned for charity; today's door is blue again.

about: South-east: Brixton market, then Deptford and Greenwich.

cards.line: Did you know, Brixton's Electric Avenue was the first market street lit by electricity?
cards.fact: Electric Avenue in Brixton was the first market street to be lit by electricity. Eddy Grant's 1982 hit song Electric Avenue is named after it.

cards.line: Did you know, a Russian emperor came to Deptford in disguise to learn shipbuilding?
cards.fact: In 1698 Peter the Great, Russia's emperor, came to the royal dockyard at Deptford, officially in disguise, to learn how ships were built.

cards.line: Did you know, a hollow oak tree in Greenwich Park was used as a prison?
cards.fact: The hollow trunk of an old oak tree in Greenwich Park was used as a prison. Anyone caught breaking the law in the park was locked inside behind a heavy wooden door.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Queen Elizabeth's Oak, Greenwich Park

cards.line: Did you know, Brixton is named after a Saxon lord's stone?
cards.fact: Brixton means Brixi's stone. Brixi, a Saxon lord, is thought to have set up a stone at the top of what's now Brixton Hill, to mark where the local court met.

cards.line: Did you know, the playwright Christopher Marlowe lies in an unmarked grave in Deptford?
cards.fact: Christopher Marlowe, one of the most famous Elizabethan playwrights, was killed in a house in Deptford in 1593. He was buried in an unmarked grave in St Nicholas's churchyard.

about: Picking someone up from Heathrow, home through Brentford and Ealing.

cards.line: Did you know, Heathrow's north runway sits on an Iron Age village?
cards.fact: Under Heathrow's north runway: an Iron Age village of 11 roundhouses and a small temple, dug up in 1944 just before the tarmac went down.
cards.source: London Museum; Grimes, Proc. Prehistoric Society 59 (1993)

cards.line: Did you know, robbers near Heathrow came for £1 million in cash and found three tonnes of gold?
cards.fact: In November 1983 six robbers broke into a warehouse by Heathrow expecting about £1 million in Spanish money. They found three tonnes of gold instead, worth £26 million. Most of it was never recovered.

cards.line: Did you know, an English army beat an invading Danish army at Brentford in 1016?
cards.fact: In 1016 the English army, led by Edmund Ironside, beat Cnut's invading Danish army at Brentford. The English lost many men, and Cnut beat them in Essex later that year.

cards.line: Did you know, Ealing has the oldest working film studio in the world?
cards.fact: Ealing Studios is the oldest continuously working film studio in the world. Films have been made on the site since 1902.

cards.line: Did you know, Ealing is named after a Saxon tribe?
cards.fact: Ealing comes from the Gillingas, a Saxon tribe named in a charter from around the year 700. The tribe took its name from its chief, a man called Gilla.
